claim: 27 hunting dogs from ten breeds were used in the study.
source: A total of 27 hunting dogs (10 M, 17 F) from ten breeds were used in the study (Supplementary file 1A- Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and composition of dogs used in the study.

claim: Dogs were equipped with GPS collars recording positions at 2.5 or 5.0 second intervals.
source: Dogs were equipped with a Garmin T5 mini (or DC50) GPS collar (Garmin Ltd., USA) fitted around the neck and programed to record GPS positions at 2.5 or 5.0 s intervals (GPS accuracy ±4.2 m based on ground-truth measurements collected at study site locations).
evidence: The manuscript describes the GPS equipment specifications used in the study.

claim: 622 trials were performed at 62 locations in the Czech Republic from September 2014 to December 2017.
source: A total of 622 trials were performed in forested hunting grounds at 62 independent locations in the Czech Republic from September 2014 to December 2017.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of trials, locations, and time period of the study.

claim: In 59.4% of cases, dogs homed by following their outbound track (tracking strategy).
source: In 399 cases (59.4 %), dogs homed by following their outbound track (tracking strategy), and in 223 cases (33.2 %), dogs homed using novel route (scouting strategy).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and counts of tracking behavior observed in the study.

claim: In 33.2% of cases, dogs homed using a novel route (scouting strategy).
source: In 399 cases (59.4 %), dogs homed by following their outbound track (tracking strategy), and in 223 cases (33.2 %), dogs homed using novel route (scouting strategy).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and counts of scouting behavior observed in the study.

claim: In 8.0% of cases, dogs combined both tracking and scouting strategies during a single return.
source: In 50 cases (8.0 %), dogs combined both strategies during a single return (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and counts of combined strategy behavior.

claim: Scouting dogs were faster than tracking dogs.
source: Scouting dogs were faster than tracking ones (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3 which shows the speed comparison.

claim: Taller dogs ran faster than smaller ones.
source: As expected, taller dogs ran faster than smaller ones, but the shoulder height did not affect length of the inbound track (Figure 4) and the average speed of the inbound trajectory was faster when a portion of the return followed forest paths (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship and references Figure 4.

claim: Shoulder height did not affect length of the inbound track.
source: As expected, taller dogs ran faster than smaller ones, but the shoulder height did not affect length of the inbound track (Figure 4) and the average speed of the inbound trajectory was faster when a portion of the return followed forest paths (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4.

claim: The average speed of the inbound trajectory was faster when a portion of the return followed forest paths.
source: As expected, taller dogs ran faster than smaller ones, but the shoulder height did not affect length of the inbound track (Figure 4) and the average speed of the inbound trajectory was faster when a portion of the return followed forest paths (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 5.

claim: Inbound track length was significantly longer when forest paths were used.
source: Inbound track length was significantly longer when forest paths were used (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 5.

claim: There was a positive correlation between direct distance between the turning point and the owner and the average inbound track length.
source: As expected, there was a positive correlation between direct ('beeline') distance between the turning point and the owner and the average inbound track length (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1B- Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correlation and references Figure 4.

claim: The compass directions in which dogs started the excursions (azimuth A) were random, irrespective of whether dogs were later tracking or scouting.
source: The compass directions in which dogs started the excursions (Figure 2A, azimuth A) and at the turning point relative to the excursion start, and thus to the goal (Figure 2A, azimuth B) were random, irrespective whether dogs were later tracking or scouting (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1E- Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 6.

claim: The compass directions at the turning point relative to the excursion start (azimuth B) were random, irrespective of whether dogs were later tracking or scouting.
source: The compass directions in which dogs started the excursions (Figure 2A, azimuth A) and at the turning point relative to the excursion start, and thus to the goal (Figure 2A, azimuth B) were random, irrespective whether dogs were later tracking or scouting (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1E- Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 6.

claim: The direction in which tracking dogs started to return (azimuth C) was random.
source: The direction in which the dogs started to return (Figure 2A, azimuth C) was random in tracking dogs, but significantly aligned along the ~north-south magnetic axis in scouting dogs (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1E- Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 7.

claim: The direction in which scouting dogs started to return (azimuth C) was significantly aligned along the ~north-south magnetic axis.
source: The direction in which the dogs started to return (Figure 2A, azimuth C) was random in tracking dogs, but significantly aligned along the ~north-south magnetic axis in scouting dogs (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1E- Table 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 7.

claim: Dogs homing by scouting started their return with a short compass run with an average length of 18.1 m.
source: Specifically, dogs homing by scouting started their return with a short (average length 18.1 m, Supplementary file 1D- Table 4), 'compass run' aligned along the ~north-south geomagnetic axis (Supplementary file 1E-F- Tables 5-6, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific average length of the compass run.

claim: The compass run was aligned along the ~north-south geomagnetic axis.
source: Specifically, dogs homing by scouting started their return with a short (average length 18.1 m, Supplementary file 1D- Table 4), 'compass run' aligned along the ~north-south geomagnetic axis (Supplementary file 1E-F- Tables 5-6, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the alignment of the compass run.

claim: The compass run was significantly oriented along the ~north-south geomagnetic axis in all four distributions when the owner was positioned at north, south, east, or west relative to the turning point.
source: In all four distributions, the compass run was significantly orientated along the ~north south geomagnetic axis, suggesting that its orientation was independent of the direction to the owner (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1F- Table 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references Figure 8.

claim: The orientation of the compass run was independent of the direction to the owner.
source: In all four distributions, the compass run was significantly orientated along the ~north south geomagnetic axis, suggesting that its orientation was independent of the direction to the owner (Figure 8, Supplementary file 1F- Table 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the data.

claim: There were no significant differences in axial preference of the compass run between sexes.
source: There were no significant differences in axial preference of the compass run between sexes (Watson's U2 test, U = 0.027, p>0.5) or between familiar and unfamiliar areas (Watson's U2 test, U = 0.036, p>0.5).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no sex differences.

claim: There were no significant differences in axial preference of the compass run between familiar and unfamiliar areas.
source: There were no significant differences in axial preference of the compass run between sexes (Watson's U2 test, U = 0.027, p>0.5) or between familiar and unfamiliar areas (Watson's U2 test, U = 0.036, p>0.5).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no differences based on area familiarity.

claim: The probability of exhibiting a scouting strategy after compass run was aligned along the north-south axis was almost four times higher than the probability of exhibiting tracking (odds ratio = 3.60, p<0.0001).
source: The probability of exhibiting a scouting strategy after compass run was aligned along the north-south axis was almost four times higher than the probability of exhibiting tracking (odds ratio = 3.60, p<0.0001) (Figure 7E, Supplementary file 1B- Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific odds ratio and statistical significance.

claim: When the compass run was aligned along the ~north-south axis, homing was more efficient compared to ~east-west compass runs (F = 6.47, p=0.01).
source: Importantly, when the compass run was aligned along the ~north-south axis, homing was more efficient, i.e., the ratio between the length of the inbound track and the shortest distance between the turning point and the goal was significantly reduced compared to the ~east-west compass runs (F = 6.47, p=0.01) (Figure 9 Supplementary file 1B- Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing improved homing efficiency.

claim: Sex and breed did not influence the probability of return strategy used during homing.
source: Sex and breed did not influence the probability of return strategy used during homing (GLMM, p>0.05).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no effect of sex or breed.

claim: The position of sun and polarization pattern did not significantly influence the orientation of azimuth C during scouting returns at the individual level (n = 251, µ = 69°/249°, r = 0.04, p=0.673).
source: The position of sun, and thus polarization pattern, did not significantly influence the orientation of azimuth C during scouting returns at the individual level (n = 251, µ = 69°/249°, r = 0.04, p=0.673) or at the group level (n = 27, µ = 146°/326°, r = 0.021, p=0.989).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no effect of sun position.

claim: The position of sun and polarization pattern did not significantly influence the orientation of azimuth C during scouting returns at the group level (n = 27, µ = 146°/326°, r = 0.021, p=0.989).
source: The position of sun, and thus polarization pattern, did not significantly influence the orientation of azimuth C during scouting returns at the individual level (n = 251, µ = 69°/249°, r = 0.04, p=0.673) or at the group level (n = 27, µ = 146°/326°, r = 0.021, p=0.989).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no effect of sun position.

claim: Less than 10% of scouting returns had wind conditions suitable for olfactory piloting to the owner.
source: Partitioning the circular data into eight equal bin sizes (each bin ±22.5° and centered on the 45's, i.e. 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, etc.), we found that the wind conditions in only 24 scouting returns (<10 % of scouting returns) were suitable for olfactory piloting to the owner (i.e. <10 % of scouting returns had wind conditions where the wind was blowing in the direction (±22.5°) from the owner to the dog at the point of return/start of azimuth C.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages based on wind direction analysis.

claim: Visual piloting is unlikely to explain the north-south alignment of the compass run because the forested habitat and dense vegetation make visual piloting unreliable and often not possible.
source: It is unlikely that the direct involvement of visual, olfactory or celestial cues can explain the highly stereotyped and consistent ~north south alignment of the compass run. For example, the forested habitat and dense vegetation of the study sites make visual piloting unreliable and, in many cases, not possible.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on habitat characteristics.

claim: There was no effect of body height on the probability of north-south alignment when compared to east-west alignment, which is not consistent with a visual piloting hypothesis.
source: Furthermore, there was no effect of the body height (and thus the degree to which the dog's field of view of its surroundings was limited) on the probability of north-south alignment when compared to east-west alignment, a fact which is not consistent with a visual piloting hypothesis.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on the lack of body height effect.

claim: Highly variable wind conditions, coupled with turbulence in the forest understory, rule out the use of olfactory piloting during scouting.
source: Highly variable wind conditions, coupled with turbulence in the forest understory, rule out the use of olfactory piloting during scouting.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on wind conditions.

claim: In many cases, the Sun's disk was fully obstructed by cloud cover and/or overhead vegetation, making it challenging to use a sun or polarized light compass.
source: In many cases, the Sun's disk was fully obstructed by cloud cover and/or overhead vegetation, making it challenging to use a sun or polarized light compass.
evidence: The manuscript describes observational conditions during the study.

claim: Polarized light has been shown to calibrate the magnetic compass in bats.
source: And, although polarized light has been shown to calibrate the magnetic compass in bats (Greif et al., 2014), detection of skylight polarization is not thought to be widespread in mammals (Horváth and Varjú, 2004; Marshall and Cronin, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on bats.

claim: Detection of skylight polarization is not thought to be widespread in mammals.
source: And, although polarized light has been shown to calibrate the magnetic compass in bats (Greif et al., 2014), detection of skylight polarization is not thought to be widespread in mammals (Horváth and Varjú, 2004; Marshall and Cronin, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on mammalian sensory capabilities.

claim: The Earth's magnetic field provides a stable, omnipresent cue, regardless of daily or seasonal temporal variation, visual cue availability or weather conditions.
source: In contrast, the Earth's magnetic field provides a stable, omnipresent cue, regardless of daily or seasonal temporal variation, visual cue availability or weather conditions.
evidence: The manuscript states a property of the Earth's magnetic field.

claim: The north-south alignment of the compass run in dogs is consistent with spontaneous magnetic alignment along the north-south magnetic axis in a range of vertebrates in the field.
source: The north-south alignment of the compass run in dogs is consistent with a wealth of studies providing support for spontaneous magnetic alignment along the north-south magnetic axis in a range of vertebrates in the field (reviewed in Begall et al., 2013; Malkemper et al., 2016) as well as in the laboratory under controlled conditions (e.g. Burda et al., 1990; Phillips et al., 2002; Muheim et al., 2006; Malkemper et al., 2015; Painter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple previous studies showing similar magnetic alignment behavior.

claim: Dogs are sensitive to magnetic cues.
source: Indeed, several recent studies have shown that dogs are sensitive to magnetic cues (Hart et al., 2013; Adámková et al., 2017; Martini et al., 2018), and behavioural studies show that Earth-strength magnetic fields play a direct role in homing responses also in the blind mole-rat, a subterranean mammal (Kimchi et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on canine magnetic sensitivity.

claim: Earth-strength magnetic fields play a direct role in homing responses in the blind mole-rat.
source: Indeed, several recent studies have shown that dogs are sensitive to magnetic cues (Hart et al., 2013; Adámková et al., 2017; Martini et al., 2018), and behavioural studies show that Earth-strength magnetic fields play a direct role in homing responses also in the blind mole-rat, a subterranean mammal (Kimchi et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on mole-rat navigation.

claim: The compass run is proposed to be mediated by magnetic cues.
source: Taken together, we propose that the compass run is mediated by magnetic cues, and it helps to increase the accuracy and reduce the complexity of long-distance navigation across unfamiliar and/or highly variable environments.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this mechanism based on the data.

claim: The compass run helps to increase the accuracy and reduce the complexity of long-distance navigation across unfamiliar and/or highly variable environments.
source: Taken together, we propose that the compass run is mediated by magnetic cues, and it helps to increase the accuracy and reduce the complexity of long-distance navigation across unfamiliar and/or highly variable environments.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this functional significance based on the observed data.

claim: In the absence of familiar landmarks, the compass run may serve to recalibrate a path integration system relative to Earth's magnetic field.
source: Noteworthy, scouting dogs in unfamiliar locations cannot use visual landmarks to recalibrate a path integration system. Therefore, in the absence of familiar landmarks, the compass run may serve to recalibrate a path integration system relative to Earth's magnetic field, so that errors accumulated during the outbound trajectory are not incorporated into the estimate of the homing direction.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on reasoning about path integration.

claim: Dogs in the study were not passively displaced as is usual in most homing experiments.
source: Importantly, dogs in our study were not passively displaced as is usual in most homing experiments (Tsoar et al., 2011; Ostfeld and Manson, 1996), and therefore, the involvement of path integration seems plausible, and may be one of several reasons why the compass run has not been identified in previous studies.
evidence: The manuscript describes a methodological difference from previous studies.

claim: The magnetic field may provide dogs and mammals generally with a 'universal' reference frame, which is essential for long-distance navigation.
source: More specifically, the research suggests that the magnetic field may provide dogs (and mammals generally) with a 'universal' reference frame, which is essential for long-distance navigation and arguably the most important component that is 'missing' from our current understanding of mammalian spatial behaviour and cognition.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this broader implication based on the findings.

claim: Homing is broadly defined as the ability to return to a known goal location after displacement.
source: Homing, broadly defined as the ability to return to a known goal location (e.g. breeding grounds, shelter sites) after displacement (Schmidt-Koenig and Keeton, 1978; Papi, 1992; Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1995), has been shown in a taxonomically diverse range of vertebrates that rely on a multitude of cues, for example visual, olfactory, acoustic, celestial, magnetic, and idiothetic (Schmidt-Koenig and Keeton, 1978; Papi, 1992; Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1995; Cullen and Taube, 2017; Lohmann, 2018; Mouritsen, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature defining homing behavior.

claim: Homing has been shown in a taxonomically diverse range of vertebrates that rely on a multitude of cues including visual, olfactory, acoustic, celestial, magnetic, and idiothetic.
source: Homing, broadly defined as the ability to return to a known goal location (e.g. breeding grounds, shelter sites) after displacement (Schmidt-Koenig and Keeton, 1978; Papi, 1992; Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1995), has been shown in a taxonomically diverse range of vertebrates that rely on a multitude of cues, for example visual, olfactory, acoustic, celestial, magnetic, and idiothetic (Schmidt-Koenig and Keeton, 1978; Papi, 1992; Wiltschko and Wiltschko, 1995; Cullen and Taube, 2017; Lohmann, 2018; Mouritsen, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on homing cues.

claim: Understanding of large-scale navigation and homing in non-migratory species, particularly in free-ranging mammals, remains incomplete.
source: However, designing systematic studies to characterize the navigational strategies and underlying sensory mechanisms mediating homing behaviour in non-migratory species, particularly in free-ranging mammals, have proven difficult, and our understanding of large-scale navigation and homing remains incomplete (Poulter et al., 2018; Tsoar et al., 2011; Wolbers and Wiener, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on gaps in knowledge.

claim: Messenger dogs were used as couriers to deliver sensitive information across battlegrounds in World War I.
source: Anecdotal accounts of the impressive navigation abilities of dogs have been commonplace, maybe best exemplified in World War I when 'messenger dogs' were used as couriers to deliver sensitive information across battlegrounds (Richardson, 1920).
evidence: The manuscript cites historical use of dogs for navigation.

claim: Nearly a century ago, the first studies designed to examine navigational abilities in dogs revealed homing success even if displaced to unfamiliar sites.
source: Nearly a century ago, the first studies designed to examine navigational abilities in dogs were performed, revealing homing success even if displaced to unfamiliar sites (Schmid 1932, 1936 cited in Nahm, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites early research on dog navigation.

claim: A comprehensive study observed consistent homing success in a total of 26 dogs displaced without exposure to visual cues in various geographic directions.
source: Decades later, a more comprehensive study observed consistent homing success in a total of 26 dogs displaced without exposure to visual cues in various geographic directions.
evidence: The manuscript describes previous research on dog homing.

claim: Dogs often homed using novel routes and/or shortcuts, ruling out route reversal strategies, and making olfactory tracking and visual piloting unlikely.
source: Dogs often homed using novel routes and/or shortcuts, ruling out route reversal strategies, and making olfactory tracking and visual piloting unlikely.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings from previous research.

claim: Hunting dogs, particularly scent hounds, have been selected over generations to detect and pursue tracks of game animals and return to the place where the pursuit started.
source: Hunting dogs, particularly the so-called scent hounds, have been selected over generations to detect and pursue tracks of game animals and, if not followed by the hunter, to return to the place where the pursuit started, often over distances of hundreds or thousands of meters.
evidence: The manuscript describes the breeding history and behavior of hunting dogs.

claim: Tracking may be safe but is lengthy.
source: While tracking may be safe, it is lengthy.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning about the tracking strategy.

claim: Scouting enables taking shortcuts and might be faster but requires navigation capability and is risky because of possible errors.
source: Scouting enables taking shortcuts and might be faster but requires navigation capability and, because of possible errors, is risky.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning about the scouting strategy.

claim: 31% of trials were carried out using a Garmin Virb Elite action camera.
source: A portion of the trials (31 %) were carried out using a Garmin Virb Elite action camera (Garmin Ltd., USA) housed inside a non-magnetic stainless steel mount fixed to the side of a custom-fitted fabric harness (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides the percentage of trials with video recording.

claim: All trials were performed with a single dog.
source: All trials were performed with a single dog (i.e. trials were not carried out with groups of dogs), in areas free from high voltage power lines, paved roads or buildings, and at different times of day (daylight hours only) and different times of year.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Trials were performed in areas free from high voltage power lines, paved roads or buildings.
source: All trials were performed with a single dog (i.e. trials were not carried out with groups of dogs), in areas free from high voltage power lines, paved roads or buildings, and at different times of day (daylight hours only) and different times of year.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental site selection criteria.

claim: Common game animals in the study region include fallow deer, red deer, roe deer, wild boar, European hare, and red fox.
source: The following game animals are common in the study region: fallow deer (Dama dama), red deer (Cervus elaphus), roe deer (Capreolus capreolus), wild boar (Sus scrofa), European hare (Lepus europaeus), and red fox (Vulpes vulpes).
evidence: The manuscript lists the game animals present in the study area.

claim: Excursions are defined as the track recorded between the excursion start and the point when the dog started its return to the owner.
source: 'Excursions' are defined as the track recorded between the excursion start (see above) and the point when the dog started its return to the owner, staying at, or within 10 m from the excursion start (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript defines the term 'excursion' for the study.

claim: In very rare cases when dogs did not return to the owner, they were found via GPS position and excluded from further analysis (n = 16, 2.4% of all excursions).
source: In very rare cases when dogs did not return to the owner, they were found via GPS position and excluded from further analysis (n = 16, 2.4 % of all excursions).
evidence: The manuscript describes data exclusion criteria.

claim: Excursions were divided into three distinct phases: outbound trajectory, turning trajectory, and inbound trajectory.
source: Based on preliminary analyses of GPS tracks used to standardize the study protocol, excursions were divided into three distinct phases: 1) outbound trajectory: from the excursion start to the point where the dog terminates its pursuit of the game track; 2) turning trajectory: the part where the dog initiates its return to the excursion start/owner; within this part, we narrowed the turning point; 3) inbound trajectory: the return track to the owner (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analytical framework for excursions.

claim: Tracking is defined as when the inbound return track falls within a ±30 m corridor limit of the outbound track.
source: Tracking: inbound return track falls within a ± 30 m corridor limit (shown by small white dots flanking each side of the track) of the outbound track.
evidence: The manuscript defines the tracking strategy with specific spatial criteria.

claim: Scouting is defined as when the inbound return track is separated from the outbound trajectory by at least 30 m.
source: Scouting: the inbound return track is separated from the outbound trajectory by at least 30 m.
evidence: The manuscript defines the scouting strategy with specific spatial criteria.

claim: The analysis of all directional data was carried out using a double-blind protocol.
source: Importantly, the personnel responsible for identifying the spatial features of excursions (i.e. excursion start, outbound, turning and inbound trajectory, turning point and owner position, see Identifying excursion features) as well as partitioning tracks into return strategy type were unaware of the directional data (azimuths A, B, C). Conversely, personnel responsible for measuring directional data were unaware to which segments and strategies each measurement belonged. Therefore, the analysis of all directional data was carried out using a double-blind protocol.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach to reduce bias.

claim: The Rayleigh test was used for circular statistics to determine if distributions were indistinguishable from random at the p<0.05 significance level.
source: The Rayleigh test was used for circular statistics to determine if distributions were indistinguishable from random at the p<0.05 significance level.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical method used.

claim: A homing efficiency index was expressed by calculating the ratio (in %) between the track length of the inbound trajectory and the direct distance between the turning point and excursion start.
source: A homing efficiency index was expressed by calculating the ratio (in %) between the track length of the inbound trajectory (i.e. track length of dog between turning point and excursion start) and the direct distance (i.e. beeline) between the turning point and excursion start.
evidence: The manuscript defines how homing efficiency was calculated.
